title: Patrol Y61 (GU)
eyebrow: NISSAN PATROL · Y61 'GU' · 1997–2016 (LATER IN SOME MARKETS)
verdict: The GU is the Patrol that kept the solid axles and coils of the GQ, added a squarer body and spent nineteen years in Australian showrooms. Buy the right engine and it's one of the great touring wagons. Buy an early ZD30 without paperwork and you might be buying a set of pistons.

paragraphs: In December 1997 Nissan replaced the [[nissan-patrol/y60|Y60 'GQ']] with a Patrol that looked new but thought the same way. The Y61, sold as the GU in Australia and the Safari in Japan, kept a separate chassis, coil springs and a live axle at each end on the wagon, at a time when Toyota was giving the [[land-cruiser/100-series|100 Series]] independent front suspension. Nissan Australia sold 104,510 GU wagons and 37,112 cab-chassis between 1997 and October 2016, according to figures quoted by JDM Buy Sell, and Middle East production carried on into 2024. Few 4x4s have had a run that long.

story.heading: SAME RECIPE, SQUARER BOX
paragraphs: Underneath, the GU is an evolution of the GQ. Wikipedia notes larger CV joints, manual gearboxes with fewer synchros, and wider axle housings to suit the new body, with the same H233 and H260 differential centres. The five-door wagon rides on a 2,970 mm wheelbase, and some markets also got a 2,400 mm three-door. Body styles were the seven-seat wagon, a cab-chassis (the UY61 in Australia), sold with either a leaf-sprung or a coil-sprung rear, and a two-door pickup. Japan also got a two-door hardtop and a four-door van.

The engine list at launch covered every taste. Australian Series I trucks offered the 4.5-litre TB45E petrol six, the 2.8-litre RD28ETi turbo-diesel six, and the 4.2-litre TD42 diesel. The TD42T turbo-diesel joined the ST in 1999. CarsGuide notes that the RD28 had a timing belt, the TD42 timing gears, and the ZD30 and petrol sixes chains. Manuals were five-speeds: the FS5R30A behind the RD28 and the FS5R50B behind everything else.

story.heading: THE ZD30 PROBLEM
paragraphs: Series II arrived in 2000 with the engine that defines the GU's reputation: the 3.0-litre ZD30DDTi, a four-cylinder turbo-diesel with a Bosch VP44 pump, rated at 116 kW. It was cheaper than the 4.2 six and could be had with an automatic. CarsGuide says it 'has a history of breaking pistons due to poor engine management and boost spikes'. Too many engines died early, usually through a holed crown or a cracked ring land on the number three or four piston, and the fix was a bottom-end rebuild.

Nobody has published a definitive cause. The suspects are the EGR system upsetting the mixture and creating hot spots, oil from the crankcase vent fouling the mass-airflow sensor, and boost spikes from a slow-reacting turbo control. Nissan also originally specified 6 litres of oil. After reports of oil starvation it raised the capacity to 8.3 litres and told dealers to shorten and recalibrate the dipsticks. In September 2004 a Nissan service bulletin, quoted by owners on ExplorOz, also tightened the oil spec to ACEA B3 or JASO DH-1 with 10W-40 strongly recommended. Owners responded with what forums call 'engine saver' mods: boost and EGT gauges, catch cans, and in many cases a blanked EGR.

story.heading: SERIES BY SERIES
paragraphs: Series III, from late 2001, brought the 4.8-litre TB48DE petrol six, a DOHC 24-valve engine rated at 185 kW in Australia, and later the intercooled TD42Ti. The 2003 Japanese facelift is credited to Junichi Sakai. The big visual change came with Series IV in October 2004: boxy wheel-arch flares, new headlights, grille and tail-lights, a new interior, and 17-inch alloys on the ST and Ti. There was no Series V; the next update was GU VI in September 2007.

By 2007 the TD42 was gone (4X4 Australia says 2006; Wikipedia says the TD42Ti couldn't meet Euro IV for 2007), and a common-rail ZD30 became the only diesel, at 118 kW and up to 380 Nm. CarsGuide suggests that the common-rail system may have helped with the boost and mixture problems. Dual front airbags only became standard across the range that year. By the end in Australia, the 3.0 was the only engine left.

story.heading: THE LONG GOODBYE
paragraphs: The petrol-only Y62 reached Australia in 2013, so the GU stayed on sale beside it until 2016. It finished with the 300-unit Legend Edition: an ST with the common-rail 3.0, a rear diff lock, and $10,000 of genuine accessories including a steel bull bar with a Warn winch, a snorkel, a roof rack and a tow bar. Because the newer truck had no diesel, late GUs held their value. Wikipedia lists a worldwide phase-out in 2014, but sales continued in South Africa, the Middle East and parts of Africa, Asia and South America. Production reportedly ended in 2024.

Its rivals were Toyota's IFS 100 Series and its solid-axle [[land-cruiser/100-series|105]], with the [[land-cruiser/70-series|70 Series]] as the cab-chassis alternative. The GU's case is simple: coil-sprung solid axles, a huge aftermarket and a truck that UN agencies and armies still drive. Pick the engine carefully and it can last for decades.

callout.label: SIDEBAR · THE DESERT PATROL
callout.title: Super Safari: the Y61 that refused to retire
paragraphs: Outside Australia the Y61 lived on as the Patrol Safari and Super Safari, built in Japan until 2024 for markets such as the Gulf. A 2017 Middle East brochure lists the TB48DE at 280 hp (SAE gross), a five-speed automatic, a rear differential lock, VDC, an electric winch and tan leather. Wikipedia notes that the TB48DE has a following among Middle Eastern tuners, and that the Gulf had special editions with names like Falcon, Gazelle and Al Ostoura.

Japan's version was the Safari, and it took a different route: the 245 PS TB48DE in the Granroad Limited from November 2002, and a rear limited-slip diff on every model from September 1999. The Safari name disappeared from Japanese showrooms in the mid-2000s, while the Gulf trucks kept going for most of another twenty years.

engineering_intro: The GU is a traditional ladder-frame 4x4 with a beam axle and coil springs at each end on the wagon. The front axle is located by radius arms and a panhard rod, which is why lifted GUs need caster correction. Drive is part-time 4WD with low range and auto-locking free-wheel hubs as standard on many trucks. The engine range is the main thing that separates good GUs from expensive ones.

engineering.v: Ladder frame · 2,970 mm (5-door) / 2,400 mm (3-door, some markets)
engineering.note: Wagon, UY61 cab-chassis and two-door pickup. Cab-chassis trucks came with either leaf or coil rear suspension.

Radius arms and a panhard rod at the front. Lifts of about 2 in or more usually need caster-correction bushes. Series 2-on wagons use a different front panhard rod and bushes from GQ and early GU trucks (per Patrolapart's listings), so order for your build.
Wider housings than the GQ, with the same centres. Some GUs have an H233B rear and some an H260, so check before you buy a locker.
Engaged mechanically (CarsGuide). Auto-locking hubs can unlock when you rock a stuck truck, so many owners fit manual hubs.

buying_checks.head: Identify the engine and series first
buying_checks.body: Make sure the engine and gearbox match the build date and series. A 'Series III ZD30' and a 'Series IV TB48' are different buys. A ZD30 sold as 'overhauled' should come with an itemised list: head, bores, pistons, bearings and rings, not just new pistons and a turbo.

buying_checks.head: ZD30: demand oil history and check the dipstick
buying_checks.body: Look for regular oil changes and the right grade: a September 2004 Nissan bulletin, quoted by owners, calls for ACEA B3 or JASO DH-1 oil with 10W-40 strongly recommended. Nissan Europe's Y61 service manual schedules ZD30 oil and filter every 15,000 km or 12 months, or every 7,500 km or 6 months in severe use such as towing, dust or short trips. Check your own market's service book; many owners change it more often. Fuel in the oil is bad news. One forum veteran says heavy soot within 5,000 km points to an open EGR, and another warns that factory intercoolers eventually leak, so check for oil staining. Listen for knocks on a cold start.

buying_checks.head: Cooling under load
buying_checks.body: Every GU engine can overheat when towing, and the TD42 has a particular reputation for it. Check the radiator core, the foam seals between condenser and radiator, and the fan clutch (it should drag and turn only about half a revolution when cold). Watch the temperature gauge on a long climb.

buying_checks.head: Manual gearbox
buying_checks.body: Drive through every gear. Owners report fifth-gear spline and hub problems and worn 2nd-to-3rd synchros on the five-speed.

buying_checks.head: Rear axle seals, diffs and underbody
buying_checks.body: Put it on a hoist. Look for wet rear backing plates from leaking axle seals, bash plates pushed up into what they're meant to protect, and damage to sills and bumpers. Find out whether the rear diff is an H233B or an H260 if you plan to fit a locker.

buying_checks.head: Cab-chassis: look behind the cab
buying_checks.body: ExplorOz members report cracks in GU cab-chassis frames just behind the cab and near the rear axle on heavily loaded trays, repaired by plating. Check under any big service body.

buying_checks.head: Rear barn door and dash
buying_checks.body: Owners report cracks in the big rear door that carries the spare, down the side of the window on the left-hand side. Dashboard tops can blister; Nissan Japan extended the warranty to seven years on specified wagons built August 2004 to June 2007.

buying_checks.head: Previous lift work
buying_checks.body: A lifted GU that wanders or steers vaguely probably needs caster correction. Lifts of about 3 in or more also need longer panhard rods, drag-link changes and longer brake lines. Ask what was fitted and whether it was certified.

repairs.title: ZD30 'engine saver' setup (gauges, oil level, breather)
repairs.time: ≈ Half a day to a day
repairs.symptoms: None until a piston fails, usually number three or four. Warning signs include high EGTs when towing, boost spikes or drops under load, sooty oil, and oil consumption.
repairs.fix: Make sure the dipstick and service fill reflect Nissan's revised 8.3-litre capacity (a Nissan representative quoted on ExplorOz advised 9 litres at a change), use ACEA B3 or JASO DH-1 10W-40 oil, then check the oil daily on hard trips. Fit a boost gauge and a pyrometer (EGT gauge) and learn what's normal. One owner saw 300–450 °C at highway speed with the EGR working and about 600 °C on a steep climb at full throttle. Back off before EGTs climb. Fit a catch can so crankcase oil doesn't reach the intake and MAF sensor, and keep the MAF clean. Blanking the EGR is common but disputed: one owner saw lower highway boost and higher EGTs after blanking it and refitted the valve. It is also an emissions device, so check your local rules.
repairs.tools: Pyrometer probe drilled into the exhaust manifold (pre-turbo) · boost gauge tee into the intake · catch can kit · MAF cleaner

repairs.title: Front wheel bearing service and hub seals
repairs.symptoms: Play in the wheel when rocked top to bottom, grinding, grease on the inside of the rim, or an auto hub that runs hot after a drive.
repairs.fix: Put the axle on stands and remove the wheel. Set the auto-locking hub to LOCK, remove its six 8 mm Allen bolts and pull the hub. Undo the two 22 mm caliper (torque member) bolts and tie the caliper out of the way. Remove the snap ring, washer and thrust ring, the lock-washer screws and lock washer, then the bearing lock nut. Pull the hub, catching the outer bearing, then lever out the seal and remove the inner bearing. Clean and repack both bearings, and fit a new seal. On reassembly, the Gregory's manual quoted on ExplorOz says to torque the lock nut to 167–196 Nm while rotating the hub, back it off, retighten to 3–5 Nm, then check the preload with a spring gauge (0–18.6 N starting force). Nissan's own Y61 service manual (FA section) gives the same figures, with zero axial end play. A Lonard's procedure gives different figures, so follow the Nissan ones.
repairs.tools: 8 mm Allen key · 22 mm socket and breaker bar · GU hub-nut socket · circlip pliers · seal driver (the old seal flipped over works) · wheel-bearing grease · spring gauge

repairs.title: Cure overheating under load (TD42 and others)
repairs.symptoms: Temperature gauge climbs when towing or climbing in fifth gear on hot days, and the A/C cuts out because of the radiator temperature sensor.
repairs.fix: Clean the radiator core thoroughly. Owners note that blocked internal tubes won't clear with a flush, so a recore or new radiator may be needed. Refit or replace the foam seals between the condenser and radiator so air can't bypass the core. Check the viscous fan clutch: when cold it should drag and spin only about half a turn. Check that the underbody air dam and wheel-well rubbers are in place, especially on lifted trucks. Fit a new thermostat and coolant at the correct mix. Fit an EGT gauge and drive by it: drop from fifth to fourth when towing, and back off when temperatures climb past what you've learned is normal. One ZD30 owner sees 300–450 °C at highway speed and about 600 °C on a long, steep climb.
repairs.tools: Radiator brushes and fin comb · coolant pressure tester · EGT gauge

repairs.title: Caster correction after a lift
repairs.time: ≈ Half a day (bushes) to a full day (arms)
repairs.symptoms: Light, wandering steering that won't self-centre after a suspension lift.
repairs.fix: Lifting a radius-arm front axle rotates it and reduces caster. One owner with a nominal 2 in kit (closer to 3 in in practice) fitted 2° caster-correction bushes and reported a clear improvement. Press the old radius-arm bushes out at the chassis end and press in offset bushes, set to add caster. For lifts of about 3 in or more, forum members also recommend an adjustable or longer panhard rod to re-centre the axle, drag-link changes and longer brake lines. Get a wheel alignment afterwards. Series 2-on wagons use a different front panhard rod from GQ and Series 1 trucks, so order for your build.
repairs.tools: Bush press or a shop press · jacks and stands · alignment afterwards

repairs.title: Rear axle seal and bearing leak
repairs.symptoms: Wet backing plate or inner rim, oily brake shoes or pads, a falling diff oil level.
repairs.fix: Rear axle oil seals are a known GU leak. Drain or lower the diff oil, remove the wheel and brake, and undo the axle retainer. Pull the axle with a slide hammer, then replace the inner oil seal in the housing. If the bearing is rough, have the bearing and collar pressed off and on at a shop. Clean contaminated brake parts or replace them, refit the axle and refill with LSD-rated gear oil if the diff is a limited-slip. Nissan's Y61 service manual specifies Nissan Hypoid LSD gear oil (KLD31-14002), or API GL-5 SAE 140 with 10% by volume of LSD friction modifier (38469-C6000), which matches what an owner quoted on ExplorOz. A non-LSD diff takes API GL-5, with 80W-90 preferred in cold and warm climates.
repairs.tools: Slide hammer · seal puller and driver · access to a press · brake cleaner

repairs.title: Fit a rear locker
repairs.symptoms: Not a fault. The rear LSD on many GUs isn't enough on rocky climbs and cross-axle ruts.
repairs.fix: First find out which rear diff you have. Harrop's GU ELocker and the Detroit H233 unit suit the H233B only, and the GU used both H233B and H260 rear centres. Remove the axles and carrier, swap the ring gear onto the locker, and fit new carrier bearings. Set preload and backlash and check the tooth pattern before refilling. Air lockers need a compressor and air line, and electric lockers need wiring to a dash switch. Shops usually do this, because a bad setup ruins the ring and pinion.
repairs.tools: Bearing puller and press · dial indicator · inch-pound torque wrench · marking compound

repairs.title: Swap auto-locking hubs for manual hubs
repairs.symptoms: Front drive drops out when you rock a stuck truck back and forth. CarsGuide notes this is a known trait of the auto hubs.
repairs.fix: With the axle on stands, remove the six Allen bolts holding each auto hub (as in the bearing service above), pull the hub assembly and fit the manual hub kit according to its instructions. Check the bearing preload while you're there. Run both hubs in LOCK whenever you're in 4WD.

faq.q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
faq.a: 265/75R16 is the popular stock-height size on ExplorOz, and some owners run 285/75R16 (about 33 in) on 16-inch rims. One owner runs 305/70R16 on a 2004 GU with only a 'tiny' scrub at full lock in reverse. Bigger sizes such as 305/70R17 and 35s are generally reported with at least a 2 in lift and the mud flaps removed. Many GUs won't take 15-inch rims over their brakes. In Australia, check your state's current limit on tyre-diameter increases; owners note Nissan sold a replacement tyre placard for 265/75R16.

CarsGuide says it would be 'very leery of any RD28 or ZD30-powered example, especially if it has covered a lot of kilometres', and that the 4.2 diesel and petrol sixes 'seem to offer a better package'. It names injection-pump failures and blown head gaskets as the RD28's problems, and calls the petrols 'guzzlers'. Owners describe the TD42T as very reliable if it's kept cool and full of oil.

faq.q: Which years are the best to buy?
faq.a: For a touring diesel, the TD42 years. CarsGuide calls the TD42 turbo-diesel 'the pick of the Patrol engines from this era', and Westside Auto names the 2005–07 TD42T ST and ST-L as the GU's sweet spot for reliability. The TD42T arrived in 1999 and the intercooled TD42Ti in 2003, and Australian sources date the end of the TD42 to 2006 or 2007. Be wary of 2000–2003 ZD30s. In the Gulf, where petrol GUs dominate, CarSwitch rates the 2008–10 Safaris as the most refined Y61s.

faq.q: Is the ZD30 really that bad, and which years were fixed?
faq.a: Nobody agrees on a cut-off and no failure rate has been published. Typical failures are a holed or cracked number three or four piston, and Nissan raised the oil capacity to 8.3 L and recalibrated the dipsticks. Perth dealer Westside Auto says the 2000–2003 engines earned the reputation for 'grenading' and calls the 2007-on common-rail engine improved. One forum veteran says most bugs were ironed out by 2003, but CarsGuide was still answering piston-failure questions about 2008 and 2009 ZD30s in 2022 and 2025. Many high-mileage ZD30s run fine. Buy on service history and condition, not on the year alone.

faq.q: Should I blank the EGR on a ZD30?
faq.a: It's the most argued-about ZD30 mod. Some owners blank it to keep soot out of the intake and report quicker spool. Others have seen highway boost drop and EGTs rise after blanking it, and refitted it. If you do it, fit boost and EGT gauges so you can see the effect. The EGR is an emissions control device, so check your local roadworthiness rules.

faq.q: How much can a GU tow?
faq.a: CarsGuide lists braked towing limits of 3,500 kg for the 4.2 turbo-diesel and 4.8 petrol wagons, 3,200 kg for the 3.0 diesel wagon, 3,140 kg for the 4.5 petrol, 2,800 kg for the 2.8 diesel, and up to 2,500 kg for the cab-chassis and ute, all with a suitable heavy-duty towbar. The 2016 Legend Edition is rated at 3,200 kg as a manual and 2,500 kg as an auto.

faq.q: What fuel economy should I expect?
faq.a: Nissan Australia quoted 17.2 L/100 km (ADR combined) for the 4.8-litre petrol, and CarsGuide expects at least 15 L/100 km on a highway cruise from the petrols and 20-plus in town. A 2010 common-rail ZD30 DX cab-chassis is listed at 12.5 L/100 km combined (15.9 urban, 10.5 highway), and the 2012 ST manual wagon at 10.9 L/100 km. A loaded touring truck on big tyres will use more.
faq.src: JDM BUY SELL / CARSGUIDE / NISSANPATROL.COM.AU / CAREXPERT

faq.a: Japanese Safaris had a rear LSD as standard from September 1999, and later Australian cab-chassis list an LSD as standard. A factory rear diff lock is documented on the 2016 Legend Edition and the Middle East Super Safari. For everything else, ARB Air Lockers, Harrop ELockers and Detroits are the usual upgrades. Check whether your rear diff is an H233B or an H260 before you order.

faq.q: What oil does a ZD30 take, and how much?
faq.a: Nissan's September 2004 service bulletin, quoted by owners on ExplorOz, requires ACEA B3 or JASO DH-1 oil and strongly recommends 10W-40. The capacity was raised from 6 L to 8.3 L, and dealers recalibrated the dipsticks, so make sure yours has been done and fill to the revised mark. A Nissan representative quoted on ExplorOz advised using 9 L at changes and checking the oil daily when working hard. Confirm the change interval in your handbook.

faq.q: How do I tell the series apart?
faq.a: Series I–III (1997–2004) have the original smooth arches and smaller tail-lights; GU III (October 2001) got a new nose. The October 2004 Series IV facelift added box-style flares, new headlights, grille and tail-lights, and 17-inch alloys on the ST and Ti. There was no Series V; GU VI arrived in September 2007 and GU VII in 2010. A diesel GU built from 2007 has the common-rail ZD30, because the TD42 had gone by then.

faq.q: Can I import one to the US or Canada?
faq.a: The US 25-year exemption counts from each vehicle's month of manufacture, so early GUs from 1997 to 2001 are now eligible. EPA rules also require the original engine configuration or a certified replacement. Canada's limit is 15 years. Bring a Trailer has sold several Y61-era Safaris and Patrols.

faq.q: Why does the front drive drop out when I'm stuck?
faq.a: CarsGuide says the standard auto-locking hubs 'have the potential to disengage when, for instance, rocking back and forth to free a stuck vehicle'. That's why many owners fit manual hubs and lock them whenever they're in 4WD. The GU's transfer case is engaged mechanically, so follow the owner's-manual procedure for shifting into 4WD.

mods.why: A 2 in lift with new coils and shocks clears 33s and makes up for touring weight. Plan for caster correction on the radius-arm front axle.

who.name: Ironman 4x4 Patrol Y61 GU lift kit

mods.why: Offset radius-arm bushes restore caster, and an adjustable panhard rod re-centres the axle on taller lifts.
The factory LSD gives up on cross-axle climbs. A rear locker is the biggest single traction upgrade, and a front one for serious rock work.
Boost and EGT gauges are what owners use to keep a ZD30 or a towing TD42 alive.
The GU is a touring truck, so bull bars, winches, rock sliders, roof racks and drawers all have a big aftermarket.

baseline_service.intro: Assume nothing has been done without receipts. On a GU, the job that matters most depends on the engine. A ZD30 needs proof of frequent oil changes and the revised oil level. A TD42 needs a cooling system that can cope with towing. Every GU needs the diff, transfer and hub servicing that bush trucks skip. Fluids and capacities below come from Nissan's Y61 service manual unless marked. Its maintenance schedules are the European ones, so check your own market's service book, and fill to the plug rather than by volume.

items.spec: ZD30: ACEA B3 or JASO DH-1, 10W-40 strongly recommended (Nissan bulletin, Sept 2004), revised capacity 8.3 L. TB48: owner's manual says 5W-30. Nissan's 2002 service manual: ZD30 outside Europe API CD, CE, CF, CF-4 or JASO DH-1 (in Europe API CF-4 or ACEA B3; never API CG-4), 8.2 L with filter. TD42/TD42T: API CC to CF-4 or JASO DH-1, 10.5 L with filter. TB45: 7.6 L, and TB48DE: 6.8 L with filter (petrol API SE to SL or ILSAC). Nissan Europe's 2004 supplement prefers 5W-30 for diesels there, so the grade depends on market and climate
items.interval: Nissan Europe schedule: ZD30 and TB48 every 15,000 km or 12 months, RD28 every 10,000 km or 6 months, halved in severe use such as towing, dust or short trips. Other markets: [CONFIRM IN MANUAL]. Many owners change ZD30 oil more often when towing
items.note: On a ZD30, confirm the dipstick has been recalibrated to the revised capacity. Sludge or grit under a cold oil filler cap is a bad sign.

items.spec: ZD30: spin-on filter with water-drain cock. Screw it on until it seats, then turn a further 2/3 of a turn, and bleed the air afterwards (Nissan service manual)
items.interval: Replace at purchase. Nissan Europe schedule: ZD30 every 45,000 km or 36 months (every 22,500 km in dusty or extreme conditions); RD28 every 40,000 km. Drain the water trap regularly
items.note: Early ZD30s are known for fuel-pump and fuel-system trouble (the Bosch VP44 pump), and clean fuel is cheap insurance.

Genuine Nissan fuel filter, GU ZD30 common-rail

items.interval: Test if cold starts are slow
items.note: Worn glow plugs are a common cause of hard starting on older diesels.

Genuine glow plug, GU ZD30 (VP44)

items.spec: RD28: belt. ZD30 and TB45/TB48: chain. TD42: gears
items.interval: RD28 belt: Nissan Europe's schedule replaces it at 80,000 km or 48 months (90,000 km for high-mileage use). Replace it if there's no record
items.note: Only the 2.8 RD28 has a belt to budget for. Wikipedia warns the RD's crank/balancer bolt can work loose, so use thread-locker on reassembly.

parts.name: Timing belt kit, RD28 (GQ/GU)

items.spec: Ethylene-glycol Nissan Genuine Engine Coolant or equivalent (L2N in Europe), at a 50% mix (Nissan's L2N comes premixed; 50% protects to −35 °C). Capacity with front heater ≈ 12.7–13.2 L (ZD30), 15.1 L (TD42), 12.0 L (TB45), 13.0–13.8 L (TB48) (Nissan service manual)
items.interval: Flush and refill at purchase. Nissan Europe: first at 90,000 km or 60 months, then every 60,000 km or 48 months
items.note: Clean the core, refit the condenser foam seals and check the fan clutch (about half a turn when cold). This matters most on a TD42 that tows.

Genuine Nissan 76.5° thermostat, GQ/GU TD42
Genuine Nissan thermostat, GU ZD30 (VP44)
Genuine Nissan thermostat, GU ZD30 common-rail

items.spec: API GL-4. Nissan's service manual lists the FS5R30A at 5.1 L (75W-90), and the FS5R50B at 3.8 L in the 1998 edition (also the handbook figure quoted on ExplorOz) but 3.5 L in the 2001–02 supplements, which give 75W-90 and then 75W-85. Check which gearbox you have before filling
items.note: Check the fifth gear and the 2nd-to-3rd shift while you're under there. Both are known weak spots.

parts.name: Gear oil 75W-90 (confirm grade in manual)
Genuine Nissan diff/gearbox/transfer fill plug, GQ/GU

items.spec: ≈ 3–4 L drains from the pan, about 12 L total (2001 ZD30 owner). Nissan service manual: 4-speed RE4R03A 11.8 L with converter, Genuine Nissan ATF or equivalent (Dexron III/Mercon); TB48 5-speed RE5R05A 10.4–10.7 L, Nissan Matic Fluid J only
items.interval: One owner cites Nissan at 40,000 km for ATF
items.note: A pan drain changes only about a third of the fluid. Do several drain-and-fills, or have a transmission shop exchange it through the cooler line (about 16 L).

parts.name: Dexron-type ATF

items.spec: ≈ 1.9 L (handbook figure, and also quoted by a 2001 ZD30 owner as Dexron III). Nissan's service manual confirms the TX12A transfer at 1.9 L, Genuine Nissan ATF (Dexron III) or API GL-4 (75W-90 preferred)
items.note: Nissan schedules it with the LSD oil: replace every 60,000 km (30,000 km when towing or on rough roads). Don't mix ATF and gear oil; drain fully if you switch.

parts.name: Dexron-type ATF

items.spec: Front ≈ 5.4 L (Nissan service manual; also the handbook figure on ExplorOz). Rear: 2.1 L with LSD (outside Europe); H233B 2.4 L open or 3.0 L with diff lock; H260 4.7 L open or 3.7 L with lock (Nissan service manual; the older ExplorOz handbook figure is also 2.1 L). Open diffs take API GL-5, with 80W-90 preferred in cold and warm climates. An LSD takes Nissan Hypoid LSD gear oil (KLD31-14002) or API GL-5 SAE 140 plus 10% LSD friction modifier (38469-C6000); owners also use 85W-140 LSD oil
items.interval: Change at purchase and after deep water crossings
items.note: CarsGuide says hard-used GUs need regular diff oil changes. Note whether your rear is an H233B or an H260.

parts.name: LSD gear oil 85W-140
Diff centre gasket, H233 (GQ/GU)
Genuine Nissan rear axle shaft grease seal, H233 GQ/GU

items.spec: Repack with wheel-bearing grease. Nissan's service manual (and Gregory's, quoted on ExplorOz): lock nut to 167–196 Nm while rotating, back off to zero, retighten to 3–5 Nm twice, preload 0–18.6 N at a hub bolt, zero end play. Repack the axle joint with NLGI No. 2 lithium grease
items.interval: At purchase, then Nissan Europe replaces the grease every 30,000 km on the ZD30 schedule (40,000 km on the 1998 RD28 schedule), and after water crossings
items.note: CarsGuide also recommends lubricating the front swivel joints on hard-used trucks. Auto hubs should be warm, not hot, after a drive.
